headline.statement: The paper reports 24 mediation tests from six models on one sample with no correction for multiplicity, and two of its stated findings -- one of the four loss-of-control eating outcomes named in the Abstract, and the paper's only significant between-person mediation result -- fall below the Benjamini-Hochberg threshold of 0.00625.
headline.evidence: Table 2 note: "Bold text is used to reflect significant effects, defined as p < 0.05"; no correction is mentioned in the Statistical Analyses section or anywhere else. Of the 24 printed indirect-effect p-values, five are significant uncorrected (.001, .026, .001, .001, .017); three survive Benjamini-Hochberg (threshold .00625) and three survive Bonferroni (threshold .00208). The two lost are p = .026 (Model 2, within-person, "difficulties resisting eating" -- listed in the Abstract as one of four confirmed outcomes) and p = .017 (Model 6, between-person, "feeling disconnected while eating" -- the paper's sole significant between-person mediation claim, reported as beta = 0.69).
headline.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --tests-json table2_indirect_effects.json --alpha 0.05 --family-label "24 indirect (mediation) effects in Table 2: 6 LOC eating outcomes x 2 predictors x 2 levels"

findings.title: Twenty-four uncorrected mediation tests; two stated claims do not survive correction
findings.location: Table 2, all 24 indirect (mediation) effects across Models 1-6; Statistical Analyses section; Abstract Results
findings.reported: Six MSEMs on one sample of 107 participants yielding 24 indirect effects, five significant at the stated alpha of 0.05 (p = .001, .026, .001, .001, .017). No multiplicity correction is applied, mentioned, or acknowledged anywhere in the paper.
findings.computed: Family-wise error rate up to 70.8% if independent; ~1.2 expected false positives; Benjamini-Hochberg threshold 0.00625, Bonferroni 0.00208. n_significant_uncorrected = 5, n_significant_bh = 3, n_significant_bonferroni = 3, n_claims_lost_to_correction = 2. The two lost are p = .026 (Model 2 within-person, 'difficulties resisting eating') and p = .017 (Model 6 between-person, 'feeling disconnected while eating'). Sensitivity check on the narrower family of the six within-person negative-affect indirect effects: BH threshold .0333, 4 of 4 significant results survive, 0 claims lost.
findings.assumptions: The family is my judgement, not the paper's -- I took the 24 indirect effects the paper itself reports and interprets. The FWER figure assumes independence and is an upper bound; these six models share one predictor, one mediator and one sample, so the tests are strongly correlated and the true family-wise rate is lower. The reproduction command requires a JSON file listing the 24 printed p-values (.001, .070, .052, .728, .026, .122, .210, .740, .154, .233, .060, .733, .001, .067, .164, .727, .858, .859, .380, .689, .001, .065, .017, .725), each with correction_applied = none.
findings.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --tests-json table2_indirect_effects.json --alpha 0.05 --family-label "24 indirect (mediation) effects in Table 2: 6 LOC eating outcomes x 2 predictors x 2 levels"

consequence.explanation: Under BH or Bonferroni over the 24 tests the paper loses its Abstract-level claim that emotion dysregulation mediates the negative-affect route to 'difficulties resisting eating', and its sole between-person mediation claim that participants higher in negative affect felt more disconnected while eating. findings.title: The level-1 (momentary observation) analytic N is never reported for any model
findings.location: Results; Table 2 and its note; Statistical Analyses; Participants and Procedures
findings.reported: N = 107 participants; 3131 of 4494 possible surveys completed. Table 2's note states only that 'momentary observations at level 1 were nested within participants at level 2'. No level-1 N appears anywhere in the main text or in either table.
findings.computed: No tool could be run on this: GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE all require an observation count, so none of the six single-item LOC eating means and SDs on the paper's own stated 1-5 scale (M = 2.26/2.79/2.54/2.88/3.45/2.19, SD = 1.32/1.42/1.41/1.38/1.18/1.26) could be checked for granularity. Only check_sd_range, which needs no n, could run; all six passed at 59-71% of the maximum SD for the range.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The level-1 N is logically necessarily below 3131: the paper states LOC items were shown only after a reported eating episode, that only assessments following eating episodes were analysed, that predictors were lagged twice and mediators once, and that non-consecutive surveys and overnight pairs were dropped from the lag construction.

consequence.explanation: Every coefficient in Table 2 rests on an unreported number of observations, so no reader can gauge the data volume or precision behind any of the paper's 84 estimates, and the granularity checks that would otherwise apply to six Likert means cannot be run at all.

findings.title: Printed precision of b and SE is too coarse to confirm the significance of seven reported results
findings.location: Table 2: the six within-person 'Positive affect -> Emotion dysregulation' rows; Model 2 within-person indirect effect; Models 1, 4 and 6 within-person positive-affect indirect effects
findings.reported: Positive affect -> Emotion dysregulation, b = -0.07 (SE 0.03), p = .038-.042 in all six models, bolded as significant and narrated in Results. Model 2 within-person indirect effect, b = 0.06 (SE 0.03), p = .026, an Abstract-level claim. Model 6 within-person positive-affect indirect effect, b = -0.02 (SE 0.01), p = .065, cited as evidence of no effect.
findings.computed: Achievable p-intervals given two-decimal rounding of b and SE: PA -> ED = [0.0027, 0.0633], straddling 0.05; Model 2 within-person NA indirect = [0.0093, 0.1161], straddling 0.05; Model 6 within-person PA indirect = [5.74e-07, 0.3173], spanning six orders of magnitude. All reported p-values fall inside their own intervals -- there is no disagreement -- but the intervals are too wide to confirm any of these significance decisions from the published table.
findings.assumptions: The paper reports no degrees of freedom. MSEM estimated by maximum likelihood tests coefficients with a Wald z, so df = 100000 was passed to make the t reference distribution numerically equal to the normal. Decimals taken as printed (b and SE to 2, p to 3). The reproduction command requires a JSON file of the Table 2 rows with b, se, reported_p, df and per-row decimals.

consequence.explanation: Independent verification of significance is impossible at the printed precision for the six positive-affect-to-emotion-dysregulation paths and the Model 2 within-person indirect effect; reporting b and SE to three decimals would resolve it entirely.

findings.title: Two significant between-person positive-affect effects appear in Table 2 but nowhere in the narrative
findings.location: Table 2, Models 5 and 6, Direct effects, Positive affect -> LOC eating, Between-person; Results sections 3.1.1-3.1.3; Discussion section 4.2 'Positive Affect'
findings.reported: Model 5: b = -0.50 (SE 0.12), p < .001, beta = -0.48. Model 6: b = -0.32 (SE 0.11), p = .002, beta = -0.29. Both bolded as significant. Neither is mentioned once in the Results, the Discussion or the Conclusions. The Discussion's Positive Affect section instead concludes that these data 'may collectively suggest that: (1) experiencing both low positive affect and elevated emotion dysregulation may not directly promote disinhibited DEBs in the natural environment'.
findings.computed: Both rows are arithmetically consistent with their own b and SE (Model 6: t = -2.91, p-interval [0.00197, 0.00616], reported .002 inside it; Model 5: t = -4.17, consistent with the printed '<.001'). The three Results subsections cover only affect -> dysregulation, dysregulation -> LOC eating, and indirect effects; the affect -> LOC eating direct rows are skipped entirely. These are the two largest standardized effects anywhere in Table 2 outside the affect-dysregulation submodel.
findings.assumptions: df = 100000 for the Wald z, as above. This is a narration finding, not an arithmetic one -- no number is in question. The paper's Abstract and Conclusions statements are scoped to 'momentary' (within-person) and 'mediational' pathways and are defensible on a strict reading; these two effects are between-person direct effects and are negative (protective), so the Discussion sentence about 'promoting' DEBs is not logically contradicted.

consequence.explanation: A reader following the Discussion's account of positive affect as having no demonstrated direct role would not learn that participants who generally reported higher positive affect reported substantially less inattentive and less disconnected eating.

findings.title: A Conclusions-level null claim rests entirely on p > .05, with no confidence intervals reported anywhere
findings.location: Abstract Results; Conclusions; Discussion section 4.2; Table 2 indirect effects. Also Participants and Procedures (comparison of the 5 excluded participants with the 107 retained)
findings.reported: 'All momentary mediational pathways involving positive affect as a predictor were not significant' (Abstract and Conclusions). Evidence offered: 12 non-significant indirect-effect p-values ranging .065 to .859. Separately: 'Participants without sufficient data did not differ from those in the analytic sample on baseline methodological, demographic, or psychopathological factors', a comparison of n = 5 against n = 107 with no test statistics given.
findings.computed: absence_of_evidence could not be run: it requires a confidence interval and the paper reports none anywhere, only b and SE, and states no smallest effect size of interest. The largest positive-affect mediation effect still compatible with the data is therefore unrecoverable from the published numbers. Three of the twelve paths sit at p = .065-.070 (Models 1, 4 and 6 within-person, all b = -0.02, SE 0.01), and at the printed precision the Model 6 row is compatible with p anywhere in [5.74e-07, 0.3173].
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. Deriving Wald intervals from b and SE would have been my own arithmetic, which no validated tool performed, so none is offered.

consequence.explanation: The claim promoted to the Abstract and Conclusions that positive affect plays no mediating role is an inference from non-significance for which the paper provides no interval evidence and no equivalence test.

findings.title: Predictor and mediator are near-collinear at the between-person level, and the mediator correlates .948 with the mediator of a prior paper on the same sample
findings.location: Introduction, Study Purpose paragraph; Table 2 direct effects, Negative affect -> Emotion dysregulation, Between-person (all six models)
findings.reported: 'negative urgency (i.e., a self-regulatory process that overlaps with emotion dysregulation [r = 0.948 in the present study]... Wonderlich et al. [2024])'. Table 2: Negative affect -> Emotion dysregulation between-person b = 0.95-0.96 (SE 0.10), p < .001, beta = 0.90 in every model.
findings.computed: |r| = 0.948 is within bounds, so no impossibility is involved and no forensic tool applies; the between-person beta of 0.90 is likewise admissible. The substantive point is arithmetic-free: a mediation model whose predictor and mediator correlate at beta = 0.90 at level 2 is very weakly identified as a distinct-constructs model, and the paper's sole between-person mediation result (beta = 0.69, p = .017) rests on exactly that near-collinear a-path -- the same result that is lost to multiplicity correction.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The paper discloses the .948 correlation openly and lists five prior publications from this dataset (Peterson 2020; Schaefer 2020; Wonderlich 2022, 2024), stating its extension as adding positive affect and differentiated LOC eating outcomes. This is a construct-validity and incremental-novelty consideration, not a data-integrity one.

consequence.explanation: Bears on whether the between-person mediation claim describes a mechanism between two distinct constructs or a near-identity, and on how much of the paper is new relative to Wonderlich et al. (2024) on the same participants.

findings.title: Exploratory analyses and all model fit statistics are asserted in prose with no numbers in the main text
findings.location: Results section 3.2 'Exploratory Analyses'; Results section 3.1 ('All MSEMs exhibited good fit (see Data S1)'); Measures sections; Statistical Analyses
findings.reported: A full paragraph of directional conclusions for six reverse-direction MSEMs ('indirect effects were significant for models involving momentary emotion dysregulation (predictor), negative affect (mediator), and four LOC eating dimensions') with no coefficient, standard error or p-value anywhere in the main text. 'All MSEMs exhibited good fit (see Data S1)' against stated thresholds (CFI and TLI > 0.90, RMSEA < 0.08, SRMR < 0.08), with no value shown. The emotion dysregulation MCFA 'required minor modifications' -- 'removing problematic items' -- with the items and basis in Data S1.
findings.computed: Nothing could be evaluated. Data S1 is declared in the article XML as EAT-58-1072-s001.docx but was not supplied in the paper package supplied to this review; extract_supplement returned FileNotFoundError. The missing-data analyses, the MCFAs, the six model fit statistic sets, the excluded-versus-retained comparison and every exploratory estimate are therefore unverified.
findings.assumptions: None. This records that the supplement exists in the publication but was not available here; it is not a claim that the paper omitted it. The reporting-hygiene point stands independently: an entire secondary analysis is summarised with directional significance conclusions and not one number in the main text.

consequence.explanation: The exploratory-analysis conclusions in Results 3.2 and the Discussion, and the assertion that all six models fit well, cannot be checked against any reported statistic.

findings.title: EMA compliance printed as 70.00% when the reported counts give 69.67%
findings.reported: 'Participants responded to 3131 out of 4494 possible surveys, reflecting good compliance (70.00%).'
findings.computed: grim_percentage: 70.00% at n = 4494 is attainable only from a count of 3146 (implied count 3145.80); 3131/4494 gives 69.67% (implied count 3130.97). The gap is exactly 15 surveys. The figure is printed to two decimals, asserting a precision the underlying ratio does not have.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own numbers. The most likely cause is rounding to a whole percent and then padding to two decimals: 69.67 rounds to 70 at zero decimals.

consequence.explanation: Affects only the descriptive statement that compliance was 70.00%; no reported model estimate or significance decision depends on it.

findings.title: The parent trial's registry identifier is one digit short and will not resolve
findings.reported: 'baseline EMA data from a multisite randomized controlled trial (NCT0204349) testing the efficacy of Integrative Cognitive-Affective Therapy (ICAT-BED) versus guided self-help Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Eating Disorders (CBTgsh)'
findings.computed: ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers are NCT followed by eight digits. The string printed here carries seven, so it cannot resolve to a record as written. Verified by direct read of the article XML; no arithmetic involved.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the ClinicalTrials.gov identifier format, which is a stated external convention. Almost certainly a dropped digit in typesetting. This paper is a secondary analysis and makes no pre-registration claim of its own.

consequence.explanation: The parent trial's registered protocol cannot be located from the identifier as printed, so whether these six MSEMs were pre-specified or exploratory cannot be checked.

findings.title: No power analysis or sample-size justification, with the between-person estimates resting on 107 clusters
findings.reported: No a-priori power analysis, target power, assumed effect size or sample-size justification appears anywhere. The sample size is inherited from the parent trial.
findings.computed: verify_power_analysis could not be run -- every required input is absent from the paper, and no invented inputs were supplied to force an answer. Context: the between-person half of every model is estimated from 107 level-2 units, and that is where the estimates are least stable (SEs of 0.38-0.53 on coefficients of 0.34-0.89, with one result at p = .052 and another at p = .055).
findings.assumptions: None. This is a reporting gap rather than an error; sample size inherited from a parent trial is ordinary in secondary analyses.

consequence.explanation: No basis is given for judging whether the between-person analyses were adequately powered, which matters most for the two between-person results sitting at p = .052 and p = .055.

not_checked.location: Results, paragraph 1: the six LOC eating dimension means and SDs (M = 2.26/2.79/2.54/2.88/3.45/2.19, SD = 1.32/1.42/1.41/1.38/1.18/1.26)
not_checked.reason: GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE all require the observation count, and the paper never reports the level-1 (momentary observation) N for any analysis. These are single-item Likert responses on a stated 1-5 scale and would otherwise be ideal targets for all three checks. Only check_sd_range could be run (it needs no n) and all six passed. No guessed n was substituted.

not_checked.location: Data S1 (Supporting Information): missing-data analyses, multilevel confirmatory factor analyses, all model fit statistics for the six MSEMs, the comparison of included versus excluded participants, and the entire set of exploratory reverse-direction MSEM results
not_checked.reason: The supplement is declared in the article XML as EAT-58-1072-s001.docx but was not provided in the paper package supplied to this review; extract_supplement returned FileNotFoundError. Recorded as not provided to this review, not as absent from the publication.

not_checked.location: Table 2, all 24 indirect effects: consistency of each indirect estimate with the product of its own a and b paths
not_checked.reason: No tool in the validated set performs a product check (check_summation tests sums, not products). Verifying that Model 1's within-person indirect b = 0.10 equals 0.35 x 0.28 would have required arithmetic no tool performed, so it was not done and no claim about it is made.

not_checked.location: Conclusions and Discussion: the claim that all positive-affect mediational pathways were non-significant
not_checked.reason: absence_of_evidence requires a confidence interval and the paper reports none anywhere -- only b and SE. No smallest effect size of interest is stated either. Deriving a Wald interval from b and SE would have been unaudited arithmetic; the point is recorded as finding 5 instead.

not_checked.location: Table 1 baseline characteristics: Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher and Bayesian Table 1 dispersion tests
not_checked.reason: Deliberately not run, and correctly so. These tests detect groups more similar than randomisation allows and require a between-arm baseline comparison. Table 1 here is a single-column description of one pooled analytic sample (N = 107) with no arm split and no baseline p-values. Their absence is not reassurance about randomisation; the question does not arise for this design.

not_checked.location: Table 2 p-values: GRIM-U rank-sum granularity check
not_checked.reason: Not applicable. GRIM-U applies only to Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon rank-sum p-values with known group sizes. Every p in this paper comes from a Wald test on a multilevel SEM coefficient, and applying GRIM-U to those is the single most likely route to a false accusation.

not_checked.location: Headline effect sizes (standardized betas in Table 2)
not_checked.reason: check_effect_plausibility needs a Cohen's d, or group means, SDs and ns to compute one. This paper reports standardized path coefficients from a multilevel SEM, which are not convertible to d without the model's implied variances. No external benchmark comparison was attempted.

not_checked.location: Statistical Analyses section: a-priori power analysis
not_checked.reason: verify_power_analysis needs the assumed effect size, alpha and target power. The paper states none of them, so there is no stated calculation to reproduce and no invented inputs were supplied.

not_checked.location: Exploratory MSEMs (reverse-direction pathway: emotion dysregulation -> affect -> LOC eating)
not_checked.reason: Described qualitatively across a full paragraph in Results 3.2 and in the Discussion, but every numeric estimate is in Data S1, which was not provided. No coefficient, standard error or p-value for these models appears in the main text.

not_checked.location: Model fit statistics (CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR) for all six MSEMs, and the MCFA loadings
not_checked.reason: The paper states its thresholds and asserts all six models met them, and that the emotion dysregulation MCFA required removing 'problematic items', but reports the values only in Data S1, which was not provided. Which items were removed, and on what basis, could not be checked.

not_checked.location: Table 1, Baseline age (13.35) and Baseline BMI (8.67) dispersions
not_checked.reason: check_sd_or_se declined to adjudicate because the paper states no range for age or BMI and no invented one was supplied (rulebook rule 4). Both are labelled SD by the column header 'M (SD)' and the as-SE readings (SD = 138 years, SD = 90 kg/m2) are self-evidently not what was meant, so there is no live concern.

not_checked.location: Table 1, Baseline eating disorder pathology (EDE global score) 2.69 (0.85)
not_checked.reason: GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE refused this cell by design. The EDE global score is a mean of four subscale means over items scored 0-6, so its granularity is far finer than 1/n; running GRIM here would have manufactured an impossibility out of an ordinary value.

limitations: This agent reads text and tables only and does not see figures. The paper contains exactly one figure (Figure 1), a conceptual path diagram with no axes, no error bars and no estimates, so nothing numeric was lost -- but that determination rests on the caption text, not on viewing the image.

Table 2's row labels differ between the publisher XML and the PDF. In the XML the third Direct-effects row of every model is labelled 'Positive affect -> Emotion dysregulation -> LOC eating', which would look like a systematic six-fold mislabelling; the PDF carries the correct label 'Emotion Dysregulation -> LOC Eating' with numerically identical estimates, and the Results narrative corroborates the PDF. This is an extraction defect and is not reported against the authors. All numeric values agree across both sources.

The paper reports no degrees of freedom. All regression checks passed df = 100000 so that the t reference distribution equals the normal, on the stated basis that MSEM estimated by maximum likelihood tests coefficients with a Wald z. If the software used a small-sample correction, the p-intervals would be marginally wider than reported here.

What counts as a family of tests for the multiplicity arithmetic is a judgement this tool cannot make. Two family definitions were run and both are reported; the conclusion depends on which is preferred, and the tests within either family are strongly correlated, so the family-wise error rates quoted are upper bounds.

Data S1 was not supplied to this review, so roughly a third of the paper's analytic content -- all fit statistics, all MCFA results, the missing-data analyses and the complete exploratory analysis set -- is unexamined.
The consistency of each indirect effect with the product of its own a and b paths was not checked; no validated tool in the available set performs a product check.

Table 2 (Multilevel structural equation models, 6 models x 14 coefficient rows = 84 coefficients with b, SE, p and beta) -- 68 of 84 rows evaluable, 0 inconsistent

report_markdown:
## What the paper claims

This is a secondary analysis of baseline ecological momentary assessment data from a multisite randomised trial of two binge eating disorder treatments. One hundred and seven adults with DSM-5 BED answered six surveys a day for seven days. Six two-level structural equation models test whether momentary emotion dysregulation mediates the path from momentary negative and positive affect to each of six distinct loss-of-control (LOC) eating dimensions. The paper concludes that emotion dysregulation mediates the negative-affect route to four of the six dimensions -- general LOC, difficulties resisting eating, feeling driven or compelled to eat, and feeling disconnected while eating -- but not to difficulties stopping eating or inattentive eating, and that no positive-affect mediational pathway is significant.

## The arithmetic verifies

This is worth saying plainly before anything else, because it is unusual. Every one of the 68 evaluable coefficient rows in Table 2 agrees with the p-value printed beside its own b and SE. All 26 Table 1 cells pass the checks that apply to them (31 checks run, 29 consistent, two declined for want of a stated range, one refused because the EDE global score is a multi-item composite to which GRIM does not apply). Participant flow and all three percentage columns reconcile. Statcheck finds no recomputable NHST triple because the paper reports none in prose. Duplication detection finds no improbable overlap once the six models are correctly declared as sharing one sample; the repeated a-path values across models are a structural consequence of a shared submodel, not copying. The problems here are problems of reporting and inference, not of arithmetic.

## Three sweep findings I dropped

The sweep flagged that the publisher XML labels the third direct-effects row of every model "Positive affect → Emotion dysregulation → LOC eating" -- a mediation path filed under direct effects, repeated six times. That is an extraction defect, not a paper defect: the published PDF carries the correct label, every number is identical across the two sources, and the Results narrative corroborates the PDF. It is not reported against the authors.

The sweep also noted that the BDI row reads exactly 15.00 (10.00) while every other Table 1 row carries non-round digits. GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE all confirm that combination is attainable from 107 integer totals; the BDI range used was my assumption rather than the paper's; and the rulebook says an isolated roundness signal is not escalated when it does not co-occur with something stronger. It is not carried forward.

Finally, the baseline-similarity tests were deliberately not run, and that is correct here. Table 1 describes one pooled analytic sample with no arm split and no baseline p-values, so there is nothing for Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher or a dispersion test to operate on. Their absence is not reassurance about the randomisation of the parent trial; the question simply does not arise for this design.

## What the reported numbers cannot settle

Two things struck me on reading the paper against its own table.

The first is how much of the between-person half of this model is carried by variables that are nearly the same variable. The between-person path from negative affect to emotion dysregulation is β = 0.90 in every model, and the paper itself discloses that its mediator correlates at r = 0.948 with negative urgency -- the mediator of a structurally identical analysis already published on these same 107 participants. A mediation model in which X and M correlate at .90 at level 2 is very weakly identified as a two-construct model, and the paper's sole significant between-person mediation result rests on exactly that a-path. That result is also the one that does not survive correction.

The second is the shape of the narrative. The Results are organised into three subsections covering affect → dysregulation, dysregulation → LOC eating, and indirect effects. The direct affect → LOC eating rows are never discussed, and two of them are the largest standardized effects in the whole table (β = -0.48, p < .001; β = -0.29, p = .002), bolded as significant. Meanwhile the Discussion devotes a section to positive affect concluding that low positive affect "may not directly promote disinhibited DEBs in the natural environment." On a strict reading the paper's summary statements are defensible -- they are scoped to momentary, mediational pathways -- but a reader would not learn from the prose that people with generally higher positive affect reported markedly less inattentive and less disconnected eating.

## What is missing

Two omissions matter more than their brevity suggests. No level-1 observation count appears anywhere, so nobody can say how much data any of the six models was fitted to; for an EMA paper whose entire contribution is within-person, that is a basic reporting requirement, and it is also what blocks the granularity checks that would otherwise apply to six single-item Likert means. And an entire set of exploratory reverse-direction models is summarised across a full paragraph of directional significance conclusions without a single coefficient, standard error or p-value in the main text, as are all six sets of model fit statistics. Those live in Data S1, which was not supplied to this review, and the data themselves are available only on request.

## Verdict

The numbers in this paper hold up under every check that could be run against them, and there is no indication of a data-integrity problem. But its two weakest claims -- one of the four outcomes named in the Abstract, and the only between-person mediation result -- do not survive correction for the paper's own 24 tests, several of its significance decisions cannot be reproduced at the precision it prints, and a third of its analytic content is asserted rather than shown. I would want the level-1 sample sizes, three-decimal standard errors, and confidence intervals for the positive-affect pathways before treating the mediation conclusions as established.
